reread_versions.rationale: The psalm makes the speaker's tongue a swift scribe's reed. Baruch describes the corresponding literal movement from Jeremiah's mouth to a written document. The comparison explains the oral-writing image; it does not identify the psalm's speaker with either man or attribute this royal song to Jeremiah.
reread_versions.source_text: My heart poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king; my tongue is the reed of a swiftly writing scribe.

reread_versions.rationale: The royal addressee is told to gird a sword upon his thigh. The mighty men surrounding Solomon's couch each carry a sword upon the thigh against nocturnal terror. reread_versions.rationale: The psalm describes aromatic substances coming from the royal figure's garments; the Song praises the bride's fragrant garments and then names a garden's perfumes, including myrrh. reread_versions.source_text: Myrrh, stacte and cassia come from your garments, from ivory palaces, from which they gladdened you.

reread_versions.rationale: The king's daughter is arrayed in gold and varied embroidery. Ezekiel's personified woman receives patterned coverings, gold and silver, a crown and celebrated beauty. The shared adornment imagery illuminates the splendid clothing; it does not identify the daughter with Jerusalem or turn the psalm into the same allegory.
reread_versions.source_text: All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; she is arrayed in gold-fringed, varied embroidery.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm anticipates sons succeeding the fathers and being appointed rulers. Rehoboam appoints his son Abijah as ruler among his brothers with the intention of making him king. The narrative supplies a concrete father-to-son appointment, while the psalm's plural sons and worldwide rule exceed this particular appointment and are not identified with it.
reread_versions.source_text: In place of your fathers, sons were born unto you; you will establish them as rulers over all the earth.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm warns against fear when another person grows rich; its following verse places that person's glory under death's limit. Proverbs warns a poor person against stretching to match a rich man and depicts the man disappearing from sight. Both restrain a response to another's wealth; Proverbs' pronouns are preserved rather than rewritten as wealth itself growing wings.
reread_versions.source_text: Do not fear when a person grows rich and when the glory of his house increases.

target_units.text: Do not stretch yourself, being poor, to match a rich man, but hold back in your own reflection;

reread_versions.rationale: God's claim to own the animals explains, in the psalm's sacrificial discussion, why human offerings cannot supply something independently His worshipers own. David likewise says that everything offered for the holy house already belongs to God and came from His hand. The shared reasoning concerns divine ownership underlying worship, with animals in the psalm and building resources in Chronicles.
reread_versions.source_text: For all the forest’s wild animals are Mine, beasts on the mountains and cattle.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm says ordinary enemy reproach would be bearable, before contrasting it with the close companion of verses 14-15. Micah warns against confidence in friends and intimate companions and describes enemies within the household. Both make breached closeness more disturbing than hostility from a recognized outsider; neither supplies the identity of the psalm's companion.
reread_versions.source_text: For if an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it; and if the one hating me had boasted against me, I would have hidden from him.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm joins hostility toward the speaker's words with evil thoughts against him. Jeremiah's opponents explicitly devise a design against him and propose striking him with the tongue. The comparison concerns plotted, verbal hostility; Jeremiah's final clause says they will hear all his words, so it is not treated as a refusal to listen or as the same episode.

reread_versions.relationship: figurative refuge illustrated by a tower
reread_versions.rationale: Calling God a tower of strength before the enemy uses the defensive function shown at Thebez: inhabitants flee into a fortified tower while Abimelech attacks, and his assault fails. Judges supplies a concrete illustration of the refuge image, not the psalm's historical occasion or an assertion that its figurative tower is that building.
reread_versions.source_text: Thou didst guide me, for Thou becamest my hope, a tower of strength before the enemy.

reread_versions.relationship: divinely imposed trap in communal lament
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm attributes entry into a trap and bodily affliction to God. Personified Jerusalem likewise attributes a net spread for her feet, being turned backward and continual pain to Him. The shared lament imagery joins divine agency, entrapment and suffering without identifying the community's ordeal with a particular captivity.
reread_versions.source_text: Thou broughtest us into the trap; Thou didst place afflictions upon our back.

target_units.text: From His height He sent fire; He brought it down into my bones. He spread a net for my feet; He turned me backward. He made me desolate, suffering pain all day long.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm describes God's royal processions in the holy place, followed in context by musicians and an assembly. Samuel narrates the ark's joyful procession with dancing companies, instruments, shouting and trumpet. This is a comparison of ceremonial movement associated with God's presence; it does not establish that the psalm narrates David's particular procession.
reread_versions.source_text: Thy processions were seen, God, the processions of my God, the King in the holy place.

reread_versions.relationship: appeal to God's knowledge of reproach
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm grounds its appeal in God's knowledge of the speaker's reproach and afflicters. Jeremiah asks the Lord to remember and vindicate him against pursuers and to know the reproach he received concerning Him. Both appeals bring persecution and reproach before God's knowledge, while Jeremiah's stated cause is not imposed on the unnamed psalmist.
reread_versions.source_text: For Thou knowest my reproach, shame and embarrassment; all those afflicting me are before Thee.

target_units.text: Lord, remember me and visit me and vindicate me against those pursuing me; do not delay. Know how I received reproach concerning Thee

Isaiah describes rebellious children making plans and agreements apart from God so as to add sins upon sins. The distinctive accumulation language is shared, but its agency differs: an imprecation addressed to God in the psalm and the rebels' own conduct in Isaiah.
reread_versions.source_text: Add lawlessness to their lawlessness, and let them not enter Thy righteousness.

Ezekiel is made a portent before Israel through actions subsequently explained as representing captivity. reread_versions.rationale: The psalm pictures mountains taking up peace for the people and hills in righteousness. Isaiah pictures mountains and hills leaping to welcome the people with joy. Both give the paired landforms an active role in a favorable communal scene; the differing actions remain intact, and neither landscape is converted into an identified set of human rulers.

reread_versions.relationship: wisdom reflection on the wicked's end
reread_versions.rationale: The psalmist's sanctuary insight concerns the last things of prosperous sinners, whose apparent security collapses in verses 18-20 like a dream. Zophar likewise describes the lawless person's apparent establishment ending in disappearance like a dream. This comparison follows the argument about deceptive prosperity; it neither identifies Job as wicked nor treats Zophar's accusation as a verdict on him.
reread_versions.source_text: until I enter God’s sanctuary and understand their last things.

reread_versions.relationship: wealth and the collapse of rest
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm places men of wealth and their empty hands beside troubled hearts and sleep. Job's discourse describes a rich man lying down, opening his eyes and being gone, with night and removal following. Wealth fails to secure enduring rest in both portrayals; the psalm's sleepers are not silently renamed slain warriors or identified with Job's rich man.
reread_versions.source_text: All those without understanding in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing with their hands.

target_units.text: A rich man lay down and will not do so again; he opened his eyes, and he is not.
Pains met him like water, and gloom stole him away at night.
A scorching wind will take him up, and he will depart; it will winnow him from his place.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm joins troubled, uncomprehending hearts, sleep and wealthy men finding nothing with their hands. Jesus' rich man plans repose on the strength of stored goods, but God calls him a fool and demands his soul that night. The parable develops the related warning that wealth cannot secure rest or possession; it is not asserted to narrate the psalm's event.
reread_versions.source_text: All those without understanding in heart were troubled; they slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing with their hands.

target_units.text: And I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, be glad!”’
But God said to him, ‘Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm explicitly calls people to bow, fall and weep before their Maker. Nehemiah records the people bowing with faces to the ground and weeping as they hear the law. These bodily responses correspond, but the leaders then forbid mourning on that holy day; the narrative is not treated as an unqualified command to repeat the same response.
reread_versions.source_text: Come, let us bow down and fall before Him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us.

target_units.text: Esdras blessed the Lord, the great God. All the people answered and said, “Amen,” lifting their hands, and they bowed and worshiped the Lord with their faces to the ground.
Jesus, Banaias and Sarabia were helping the people understand the law, while the people remained in their places.
They read from a book of God’s law, and Esdras taught and explained with knowledge of the Lord; the people understood the reading.

Neemias, Esdras the priest and scribe, and the Levites who helped the people understand said to all the people, “The day is holy to the Lord our God. Do not mourn or weep.” For all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the law.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm says God has not dealt with the community according to its sins. Nehemiah's confession recounts disobedience and being handed to foreign peoples, yet says abundant compassion prevented their complete destruction or abandonment. Both distinguish the people's wrongdoing from the merciful restraint of God's response; neither requires an absence of all punishment.
reread_versions.source_text: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our lawless deeds,

target_units.text: “Thou didst prolong Thy dealings with them for many years and testify to them by Thy Spirit through Thy prophets, but they did not give ear. Thou gavest them into the hand of the peoples of the land.
“In Thine abundant compassion Thou didst not make an end of them or abandon them, for Thou art mighty, merciful and compassionate.

reread_versions.relationship: contrast in provision for wild animals
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm's springs supply drinking water to beasts and satisfy wild donkeys' thirst. Jeremiah's lack-of-rain scene has empty wells, failed pasture and wild donkeys whose eyes fail for lack of grass. The contrasting scenes show wild animals receiving or lacking provision; Jeremiah's stated grass deprivation is not changed into a claim that those donkeys died of thirst.
reread_versions.source_text: They give drink to all the beasts of the field; wild donkeys will receive it for their thirst.

target_units.text: Her magnates sent their younger ones for water; they came to wells and found no water and brought back their vessels empty.
And the land’s works failed because there was no rain; the farmers were ashamed and covered their heads.
And deer in the field gave birth and abandoned their young, because there was no pasture.
Wild donkeys stood in wooded valleys; they drew in wind, their eyes failed, because there was no grass, because of a people of injustice.

reread_versions.relationship: daylight as the time for work
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm sets human labor until evening within the alternation of day and nocturnal animal activity. Jesus uses the same day-and-night limit to urge the works of His sender while it is day, before the night when no one can work. The comparison links the ordinary daily pattern with its use in His explanation of urgent work, without equating their settings.
reread_versions.source_text: A man will go out to his work and to his labor until evening.

target_units.text: We must work the works of the One who sent Me while it is day. Night is coming, when no one can work.
While I am in the world, I am the Light of the world.”

reread_versions.rationale: The speaker takes a cup of salvation in answer to what the Lord has done, within a thanksgiving and vow context. Psalm 22 praises the Lord's excellent, intoxicating cup alongside His provision and lasting mercy. The poems relate a cup to divine beneficence; this does not establish a shared ritual or identify either cup as the Eucharist.
reread_versions.source_text: I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.

target_units.text: Thou didst prepare a table before me opposite those who afflict me; Thou didst enrich my head with oil, and Thy cup is intoxicating—how excellent!
And Thy mercy will pursue me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the Lord’s house for length of days.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm asks how long the servant has and when God will judge his pursuers. Habakkuk asks how long his cry while wronged will go unanswered and describes judgment not reaching completion while the impious oppresses the righteous. Both articulate the distress of awaiting justice under oppression without identifying a common adversary or calculating a duration.
reread_versions.source_text: How many are the days of Thy servant? When wilt Thou give me judgment against those who pursue me?

target_units.text: How long, Lord, shall I cry and Thou wilt not listen? I shall cry to Thee while being wronged, and Thou wilt not save?
Why didst Thou show me toil and pain, to look upon misery and impiety? Judgment has come against me, and the judge takes.
Therefore law has been scattered, and judgment is not brought to completion; the impious oppresses the righteous, so judgment will go forth distorted.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalmist asks when judgment against pursuers will come. Jesus' widow repeatedly asks a judge for justice against her adversary, and His application concerns God's chosen ones crying day and night for justice. The parable addresses the psalm's kind of waiting appeal; it supplies neither the servant's lifetime nor an identity for the persecutors.
reread_versions.source_text: How many are the days of Thy servant? When wilt Thou give me judgment against those who pursue me?

target_units.text: And He told them a parable about their need to pray always and not lose heart,
saying, “There was a certain judge in a certain city who neither feared God nor respected any person.
And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him, saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’
For a time he was unwilling. But afterward he said within himself, ‘Even though I do not fear God or respect any person,
yet because this widow troubles me, I will give her justice, lest by coming continually she wear me down.’”
And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says.
And will not God bring about justice for His chosen ones who cry to Him day and night? And will He delay over them?
I tell you, He will bring about justice for them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?”

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm connects not turning away from God's judgments with being instructed by Him. Isaiah's speaker receives the Lord's instruction through an opened ear and answers that he does not disobey or contradict. Both make divine teaching the setting for obedient response; Isaiah's actual wording is retained rather than replaced with an expected turned-back phrase.
reread_versions.source_text: I did not turn away from Thy judgments, for Thou didst instruct me.

target_units.text: The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know the right time when a word must be spoken. He appointed morning for me; He added an ear for me to hear,
and the Lord’s instruction opens my ears. I do not disobey or contradict.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalmist reckons the earth's sinners as transgressors and therefore loves God's testimonies. Paul explains that the law makes the world answerable to God and brings knowledge of sin. The connection concerns instruction exposing wrongdoing; Paul's argument about justification is not made identical to the psalmist's declaration of love, nor is the psalm said to quote Romans.
reread_versions.source_text: I reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I loved Thy testimonies continually.

target_units.text: And we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become answerable to God;
because by works of law no flesh will be justified before Him, for through law comes knowledge of sin.

reread_versions.relationship: justice and rescue from the wrongdoer's hand
reread_versions.rationale: The psalmist claims judgment and righteousness and asks not to be handed to those who wrong him. Jeremiah's command joins doing justice and righteousness with rescuing the plundered from the wrongdoer's hand. The same cluster of just conduct and protection from an oppressor appears as a personal appeal and as a command to those responsible for justice.
reread_versions.source_text: Sixteen: Ain. I did judgment and righteousness; do not hand me over to those who wrong me.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Do justice and righteousness; rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him. Do not oppress the newcomer, orphan, or widow, and do not act impiously or shed innocent blood in this place.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm describes their full storehouses and multiplying sheep. Deuteronomy's blessing catalogue likewise joins productive flocks with blessed storehouses and storerooms. These concrete prosperity images correspond; the psalm's preceding foreigners and ensuing distinction about happiness are preserved, so its owners are not declared obedient covenant recipients merely from their abundance.
reread_versions.source_text: Their storehouses full, pouring forth from this to that; their sheep bearing many young, multiplying in their outgoing places.

target_units.text: Blessed are the offspring of your womb, and the produce of your land, the herds of your cattle, and the flocks of your sheep.
Blessed are your storehouses and your reserves.
Blessed are you when you come in, and blessed are you when you go out.
The Lord your God deliver your enemies who rise against you, crushed before your face. By one way shall they come out against you, and by seven ways shall they flee before you.
The Lord send His blessing upon you in your storerooms, and in all that you put your hand unto, upon the land which the Lord your God gives you.

reread_versions.relationship: contrast in the sound of public squares
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm's picture of their security includes no cry in their squares. Amos announces the opposite public condition: mourning in every square and road as the Lord passes through. The contrast concerns the audible sign of communal peace or distress, without identifying the psalm's prosperous group with the people addressed by Amos.
reread_versions.source_text: Their oxen fat; there is no collapse of a fence and no passage out, nor any cry in their squares.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: “In every square there will be mourning, and in every road it will be said, ‘Alas, alas!’ A farmer will be called to mourning and lamentation and to those skilled in wailing,
and in every road there will be mourning, because I will pass through your midst,” said the Lord.

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm praises God for strengthening Jerusalem's gate bars and blessing children within her. Zechariah promises a populous Jerusalem with God as a wall of fire around her and glory within. Both join Jerusalem's inhabited interior to protection provided by God; the fiery wall is not turned into the psalm's literal bars or assigned to Nehemiah's gate orders.
reread_versions.source_text: For He strengthened the bars of your gates; He blessed your children within you.

target_units.text: and said to him, “Run and speak to that young man: Jerusalem will be inhabited fruitfully because of the multitude of people and animals within her.
I will be a wall of fire around her, says the Lord, and I will be glory within her.”

reread_versions.relationship: the Lord's word pictured as running
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm says God's sent word will run swiftly. Paul requests prayer that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified. The unusual running image is shared, while the psalm's following weather and Israel-instruction context differs from Paul's request concerning proclamation; no direct quotation is claimed.
reread_versions.source_text: He sends His oracle to the earth; His word will run swiftly,

target_units.text: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, just as it also is among you,

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm extends its praise summons across young men, young women, old and younger people. Joel's summons to a consecrated gathering deliberately includes elders, nursing infants, bridegroom and bride. Both make participation span age and household stages; Joel's fast and pleading are not identified with the psalm's praise occasion.
reread_versions.source_text: young men and young women, old people with younger people.

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service.
Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

reread_versions.rationale: The psalm calls executing a written judgment glory for all God's holy ones. Paul says the saints will judge the world and angels and uses that expectation in discussing disputes. Both associate holy ones with judgment, but Paul does not identify the psalm's unnamed written judgment or prescribe its pictured weapons for church disputes.
reread_versions.source_text: to execute upon them a written judgment. This is glory for all His holy ones.

target_units.text: Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest cases?
Do you not know that we will judge angels, to say nothing of matters of ordinary life?

reread_versions.relationship: judgment and honor of the holy ones
reread_versions.rationale: The psalm attaches glory for the holy ones to judgment against the hostile nations and rulers of its context. Daniel sees the horn attack the holy ones until the Ancient of Days gives judgment to them and they receive kingship. The shared association is judgment with their vindication and honor; the psalm's particular written judgment remains unidentified.
reread_versions.source_text: to execute upon them a written judgment. This is glory for all His holy ones.

target_units.text: I observed that horn waging war against the holy ones and routing them,
until the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the holy ones of the Most High. The time was given, and the holy ones took possession of the kingship.

case.source_text: From heaven Thou didst cause judgment to be heard; the earth feared and grew quiet,
case.reason: The psalm combines judgment heard from heaven with the earth fearing and growing quiet. Zechariah calls all flesh to reverence because the Lord rose from His holy clouds, but does not state the anticipated silence or heard judgment. The remaining broad divine-appearance response does not establish the proposed particular parallel.

case.source_text: I am poor and in toils from my youth; but after being raised up, I was humbled and left helpless.
case.reason: The source explicitly places humiliation and helplessness after being raised up. The actual Job passage speaks of being placed amid pains and cast away from salvation; it does not describe the anticipated lifting by wind or that raised-then-humbled sequence. That expected alternative wording is not supplied, and shared affliction alone is insufficient.

case.source_text: I opened my mouth and drew breath, for I longed for Thy commandments.
case.reason: The source opens the mouth and draws breath in longing for commandments. Job describes hearers awaiting his speech like thirsty earth awaiting rain; the expected opening of their mouths is absent. Desire for words alone does not establish the proposed particular mouth-and-breath correspondence.

Thou camest upon me without mercy; with a mighty hand Thou didst scourge me.
Thou didst place me amid pains and cast me away from salvation.
For I know that death will wear me away; for earth is the house of every mortal.

They added nothing to my word, and became overjoyed whenever I spoke to them.
Like thirsty earth awaiting rain, so they awaited my speech.
